Thinking you need independence to add expected values. You need it only for variances.

title: AII 600 midterm study guide
text:
3. Bayes rule

The idea
You know how likely the evidence is under each explanation, \(P(E\mid H)\), and you want how likely each explanation is given the evidence, \(P(H\mid E)\). Bayes rule turns one into the other: \[P(H\mid E)=\frac{P(E\mid H)\,P(H)}{P(E)}.\] The denominator comes from the law of total probability: add up every way the evidence can happen. \[P(E)=P(E\mid H)P(H)+P(E\mid \bar H)P(\bar H).\] With more than two explanations, the sum has one term per explanation.
Three ways to compute a posterior. Use whichever you trust most under time pressure, and use a second one to check.

Counts. Imagine 1,000 people (or 100,000 if the base rate is tiny). Split them by the prior, then by the test. The posterior is “true positives over all positives”.
Formula. Bayes rule with the total-probability denominator.
Odds. Odds are \(O(H)=P(H)/(1-P(H))\), and \(P(H)=O(H)/(1+O(H))\). Then \[\underbrace{\frac{P(H\mid E)}{P(\bar H\mid E)}}_{\text{posterior odds}}=\underbrace{\frac{P(E\mid H)}{P(E\mid \bar H)}}_{\text{Bayes factor}}\times\underbrace{\frac{P(H)}{P(\bar H)}}_{\text{prior odds}}.\] The Bayes factor is the same for everyone who agrees about the test. People who disagree about the prior disagree about the posterior. The odds form also makes repeated evidence easy: if two pieces of evidence are independent given \(H\) and given \(\bar H\), multiply both Bayes factors into the prior odds.

Always say odds of what. Bookmakers quote odds against an event, which is the class Oddschecker slide’s \(O(A)=(1-P(A))/P(A)\): “2 to 1” at a bookmaker means \(P(A)=1/3\). In the island problem, “odds of innocence 1000 to 1” means \(P(I)/P(G)=1000\). Odds in favor of \(A\) of 2 to 7 mean \(P(A)=2/(2+7)=2/9\).
Test vocabulary. For a disease \(D\) and a positive test \(T\): sensitivity is \(P(T\mid D)\), specificity is \(P(\bar T\mid \bar D)\), and the false positive rate is \(1-\text{specificity}=P(T\mid\bar D)\). None of these is \(P(D\mid T)\), the number a patient wants.
The prosecutor’s fallacy is treating \(P(E\mid\text{innocent})\) as if it were \(P(\text{innocent}\mid E)\), so that \(1-P(E\mid\text{innocent})\) gets quoted as the probability of guilt. The same mistake runs the other way when \(P(E\mid\text{guilty})\) is quoted as \(P(\text{guilty}\mid E)\). The fix is always the same: bring in the base rate.


Recipe

Name the events: \(D\) for the condition, \(T\) for the evidence. Write every given number as a probability with a bar. Translate “detection rate” to \(P(T\mid D)\) and “false positive rate” to \(P(T\mid\bar D)\).
Write the prior \(P(D)\). If two people disagree, it is the prior they disagree about.
Compute \(P(T)\) by total probability.
Divide: \(P(D\mid T)=P(T\mid D)P(D)/P(T)\).
Check with counts or odds. Then say what the number means and how it moves if the prior moves.



Worked example 3.1: Alice’s mammogram (class)
Alice is 40. For women like her, 1% have breast cancer. The mammogram detects 80% of cancers and has a 10% false positive rate. Her mammogram is positive. What is \(P(\text{cancer}\mid\text{positive})\)?
Counts. Of 1,000 women like Alice, 10 have cancer and 990 do not. Of the 10, 80% test positive: 8. Of the 990, 10% test positive: 99. There are \(8+99=107\) positives, and 8 of them have cancer: \(8/107=0.075\).
Formula. \(P(T)=0.8(0.01)+0.1(0.99)=0.008+0.099=0.107\), so \(P(D\mid T)=0.008/0.107=0.075\).
Odds. Prior odds \(0.01/0.99=1/99\). Bayes factor \(0.8/0.1=8\). Posterior odds \(8/99\), so \(P(D\mid T)=8/(99+8)=8/107=0.075\).
What it means: a positive mammogram raises Alice’s probability from 1% to 7.5%, but most positives (99 of 107) come from healthy women, because healthy women vastly outnumber sick ones. What would change it: a higher prior (a family history) or a more specific test. With a 1% false positive rate, the count of false positives drops from 99 to about 10 and the posterior rises to about 45%.


Worked example 3.2: an oil field with three possibilities (book Chapter 2)
Geologists assign \(P(\text{high quality oil})=0.50\), \(P(\text{medium})=0.20\), \(P(\text{no oil})=0.30\). A soil test finds a particular soil type, with \(P(\text{soil}\mid\text{high})=0.20\), \(P(\text{soil}\mid\text{medium})=0.80\), \(P(\text{soil}\mid\text{none})=0.20\).
Total probability, one term per explanation: \(P(\text{soil})=0.50(0.20)+0.20(0.80)+0.30(0.20)=0.10+0.16+0.06=0.32\).
Posteriors: high \(0.10/0.32=0.3125\), medium \(0.16/0.32=0.50\), none \(0.06/0.32=0.1875\). They sum to 1.
What it means: the soil type is four times as likely under medium oil as under the other two, so it moves probability toward medium and away from both high and none. The chance of some oil rises from 0.70 to 0.8125. A decision can flip on this: a firm that drills only when \(P(\text{no oil})<0.20\) would not drill before the test (0.30) and would drill after it (0.1875).
A second test. Suppose a second soil sample, independent of the first given the oil type, shows the same soil. Use the posteriors as the new prior: \(0.3125(0.2)+0.50(0.8)+0.1875(0.2)=0.0625+0.40+0.0375=0.50\), so the new posteriors are \(0.125,\ 0.80,\ 0.075\). The independence assumption matters: if the second sample came from the same spot, it would mostly repeat the first one and should move you much less.


Worked example 3.3: the island and a DNA match (class)
A crime is committed on an island of 1,001 people. The criminal left a trait that occurs in 1 in 10,000 people, and a suspect has it. Before the evidence, every islander is equally likely: the prior odds that the suspect is innocent are \(1000\) to 1. A match is certain if he is guilty and has probability \(p=10^{-4}\) if he is innocent, so the Bayes factor for innocence is \(p/1=10^{-4}\).
Posterior odds of innocence: \(1000\times 10^{-4}=0.1\), so \(P(\text{innocent}\mid\text{match})=0.1/1.1=0.091\) and \(P(\text{guilty}\mid\text{match})=0.909\).
The prosecutor who says “the match probability is 1 in 10,000, so he is 99.99% likely to be guilty” reported \(1-P(E\mid\text{innocent})\), not \(P(\text{guilty}\mid E)\). The expected number of other islanders who also match is \(1000\times 10^{-4}=0.1\), and that is exactly the posterior odds of innocence. On an island of 10,001 people the posterior odds would be 1 and the suspect a coin flip.


See it move
In the Base-Rate Lab, load the Mammogram case. Predict first: of the 1,000 dots, how many test positive, and how many of those have cancer? Count the red and amber dots to check. Press Positive again and predict the new posterior before you look: the posterior odds were \(8/99\), and a second independent positive multiplies them by 8 again. Last, drag the prevalence slider and find the base rate at which one positive test gives a 50% posterior. (Answers: 107 positives, 8 with cancer; \(64/163\approx 0.39\); about 11%, where the prior odds are \(1/8\).)


Your turn
Problem 3.1 (light aircraft, book Chapter 2). 70% of light aircraft that disappear in flight are later found. Of the aircraft that are found, 60% have an emergency locator. Of the aircraft that are not found, 90% do not have a locator. An aircraft with a locator has disappeared. What is the probability that it will be found?






TipSolution





Let \(F\) be “found” and \(L\) “has a locator”. \(P(F)=0.70\), \(P(L\mid F)=0.60\), \(P(L\mid\bar F)=1-0.90=0.10\). Then \(P(L)=0.70(0.60)+0.30(0.10)=0.42+0.03=0.45\) and \(P(F\mid L)=0.42/0.45=0.933\). Watch the translation: “90% of the aircraft not found do not have a locator” is \(P(\bar L\mid\bar F)\), so you need its complement.



Problem 3.2 (blood pressure screening, book Chapter 2). A screening test for hypertension gives this joint probability table:




Hypertension present
Absent




Test positive
0.09
0.03


Test negative
0.03
0.85




What is the probability that a random person has hypertension? That a random person tests positive?
Given a positive test, what is the probability of hypertension?
Your doctor already thought you had a 50% chance of hypertension before the test. Use the test’s sensitivity and false positive rate from the table to update that prior after a positive test.







TipSolution






\(P(H)=0.09+0.03=0.12\). \(P(+)=0.09+0.03=0.12\).
\(P(H\mid +)=0.09/0.12=0.75\).
The test’s properties do not depend on your prior: \(P(+\mid H)=0.09/0.12=0.75\) and \(P(+\mid\bar H)=0.03/0.88=0.0341\). With \(P(H)=0.5\): \(P(+)=0.75(0.5)+0.0341(0.5)=0.392\) and \(P(H\mid +)=0.375/0.392=0.957\). Odds check: the Bayes factor is \(0.75/0.0341=22\), the prior odds are 1, so the posterior odds are 22 and the probability is \(22/23=0.957\).




Problem 3.3 (random HIV testing, book Chapter 2). The ELISA test has sensitivity 0.993 and specificity 0.9999. In the general population, the probability that a random person has HIV is 0.000025.

Find the probability that a random person tests positive.
A random person tests positive. What is the probability that they have HIV?
The person is retested, and the second test, independent of the first given their status, is also positive. Update the probability using the odds form.
What problem does (b) create for a policy of testing everyone at random? What would change it?







TipSolution






\(P(T)=0.993(0.000025)+0.0001(0.999975)=0.0000248+0.0001000=0.0001248\).
\(P(H\mid T)=0.0000248/0.0001248=0.199\). About four of every five positives are false.
Bayes factor \(0.993/0.0001=9{,}930\). Prior odds \(0.000025/0.999975=0.000025\). Two independent positives: posterior odds \(0.000025\times 9{,}930^2=2{,}465\), so the probability is \(2{,}465/2{,}466=0.9996\).
Most people flagged by a single test are healthy, which brings anxiety, stigma, and follow-up costs. Two remedies follow from Bayes rule: test groups with a higher base rate, which raises the prior, or confirm every positive with a second independent test, which multiplies the Bayes factor.




Problem 3.4 (the jury, book Chapter 2). A jury reaches the correct verdict with probability 0.95, whether the defendant is innocent or guilty. 80% of defendants brought to trial are guilty.

Given an “innocent” verdict, what is the probability that the defendant is innocent?
Given a “guilty” verdict, what is the probability that the defendant is guilty?
Do the answers to (a) and (b) sum to one? Should they?







TipSolution






\(P(\text{verdict innocent})=0.95(0.20)+0.05(0.80)=0.19+0.04=0.23\). \(P(I\mid VI)=0.19/0.23=0.826\).
\(P(G\mid VG)=0.95(0.80)/(1-0.23)=0.76/0.77=0.987\).
No, \(0.826+0.987\ne 1\), and there is no reason they should: they condition on different events. What does sum to one is \(P(I\mid VI)+P(G\mid VI)\). Even with a 95% accurate jury, about 1 in 6 “innocent” verdicts goes to a guilty defendant, because guilty defendants are the majority.




Problem 3.5 (a DNA match in a city). A DNA profile matches 1 in 10,000 people. The crime happened in a city with 500,000 adults, and before the DNA evidence any of them could have done it.

A suspect found by searching a database matches. Treat every adult as equally likely a priori. What are the prior odds of innocence, the Bayes factor, the posterior odds, and \(P(\text{guilty}\mid\text{match})\)?
Other evidence narrows the pool to 2,000 people before the DNA test. Recompute \(P(\text{guilty}\mid\text{match})\).
A newspaper writes that “the chance an innocent person matches is 1 in 10,000, so the suspect is almost certainly guilty.” Name the error in one sentence.







TipSolution






Prior odds of innocence \(499{,}999\approx 500{,}000\). Bayes factor \(P(E\mid I)/P(E\mid G)=10^{-4}/1\). Posterior odds of innocence \(500{,}000\times 10^{-4}=50\). \(P(\text{guilty}\mid\text{match})=1/51=0.020\). About 50 other adults in the city match.
Posterior odds \(2{,}000\times 10^{-4}=0.2\), so \(P(\text{guilty}\mid\text{match})=1/1.2=0.833\). Same DNA evidence, very different conclusion: the prior does the rest.
It is the prosecutor’s fallacy: \(P(\text{match}\mid\text{innocent})=10^{-4}\) is not \(P(\text{innocent}\mid\text{match})\), which depends on how many people could have matched.






Traps

Reporting the sensitivity, or one minus the false positive rate, as the answer. The answer has the base rate in it.
Translating “90% of the not-found aircraft do not have a locator” into \(P(L\mid\bar F)=0.90\). Read each sentence twice and write it with a bar.
Forgetting a term in \(P(E)\) when there are three or more explanations.
Multiplying Bayes factors for repeated tests without saying the tests are independent given the truth.

title: AII 600 midterm study guide
text:
4. Expectation and variance

The idea
The expected value is the probability-weighted average of the values: \[E(X)=\sum_x x\,P(X=x).\] It is the long-run average over many repetitions, not the value you expect to see next time. A $1 bet with expected value \(-\$0.03\) never pays \(-\$0.03\).
The variance measures spread around the mean, and the standard deviation is its square root, back in the units of \(X\): \[Var(X)=E\big((X-E(X))^2\big)=E(X^2)-E(X)^2, \qquad sd(X)=\sqrt{Var(X)}.\]
Covariance measures whether two variables move together, and correlation rescales it to lie between \(-1\) and \(1\) with no units: \[Cov(X,Y)=E\big((X-E(X))(Y-E(Y))\big), \qquad Corr(X,Y)=\frac{Cov(X,Y)}{sd(X)\,sd(Y)}.\] Independent variables have zero covariance. The converse is false: if \(X\) is \(-1\), 0, or 1 with equal probability and \(Y=X^2\), the covariance is zero but \(Y\) is a function of \(X\). Correlation sees only straight-line dependence.
Rules for combinations. For constants \(a\) and \(b\): \[E(aX+bY)=aE(X)+bE(Y), \qquad Var(aX+bY)=a^2Var(X)+b^2Var(Y)+2ab\,Cov(X,Y).\] Three consequences you will use:

Constants come out squared: \(Var(3X)=9\,Var(X)\), and adding a constant does not change the variance.
For independent variables, variances add even when you subtract: \(Var(X-Y)=Var(X)+Var(Y)\).
For \(n\) independent copies with mean \(\mu\) and standard deviation \(\sigma\), the total has mean \(n\mu\) and standard deviation \(\sqrt{n}\,\sigma\), and the average has mean \(\mu\) and standard deviation \(\sigma/\sqrt{n}\).



Recipe

Write the distribution as a table of values and probabilities.
\(E(X)\): multiply each value by its probability and add.
\(Var(X)\): compute \(E(X^2)\) the same way, then subtract \(E(X)^2\). A variance can never be negative; if yours is, recheck.
For a portfolio or any combination \(aX+bY\), write the formula first, then plug in. Do not forget the covariance term, and do not forget that the weights are squared.
Interpret: the mean is the long-run average; the standard deviation is the typical distance from it.



Worked example 4.1: two roulette bets (class)
European roulette has 37 pockets: 18 red, 18 black, and a zero. Compare two $1 bets.

Black pays even money: net \(W=+1\) with probability \(18/37\) and \(-1\) with probability \(19/37\). \(E(W)=(18-19)/37=-0.027\). \(E(W^2)=1\), so \(Var(W)=1-0.027^2=0.999\) and \(sd(W)=1.00\).
A single number pays 35 to 1: \(W=+35\) with probability \(1/37\) and \(-1\) with probability \(36/37\). \(E(W)=(35-36)/37=-0.027\), the same. \(E(W^2)=(1225+36)/37=34.08\), so \(sd(W)=5.84\).

Same mean, very different risk. Both lose 2.7 cents per dollar in the long run. The single-number bet swings much more, so it ends an evening faster in either direction. If your goal is to stay at the table, bet on black.
In class we used the payout including the returned stake, \(X=W+1\), so \(E(X)=0.973\). The variances, 1 and 34, are the same as here, because adding a constant shifts a distribution without spreading it.


Worked example 4.2: Tortoise and Hare split the leads (class)
Tortoise sells 1 or 2 cars a day with equal probability; Hare sells 0 or 3. \(E(T)=E(H)=1.5\), \(Var(T)=0.25\), \(Var(H)=2.25\). When one has a good day the other has a bad one: \(Cov(T,H)=-0.75\). Split the leads, \(P=\tfrac12 T+\tfrac12 H\).

\(E(P)=\tfrac12(1.5)+\tfrac12(1.5)=1.5\).
\(Var(P)=\tfrac14(0.25)+\tfrac14(2.25)+2\cdot\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12(-0.75)=0.0625+0.5625-0.375=0.25\).

Without the covariance term you would get 0.625, worse than Tortoise alone. The negative covariance cancels Hare’s noise.


Worked example 4.3: a two-country portfolio (book Chapter 1)
Monthly returns: US mean 1.15%, sd 3.30%; Hong Kong mean 1.70%, sd 7.51%; correlation 0.3. Invest 75% in the US and 25% in Hong Kong.

\(E(R_p)=0.75(0.0115)+0.25(0.0170)=0.012875\), about 1.29% a month.
\(Var(R_p)=0.75^2(0.033)^2+0.25^2(0.0751)^2+2(0.75)(0.25)(0.3)(0.033)(0.0751)=0.000613+0.000353+0.000279=0.001244\), so \(sd(R_p)=0.0353\), about 3.53%.

The mean is the weighted average of the means, but the standard deviation, 3.53%, is below the weighted average of the standard deviations, \(0.75(3.30)+0.25(7.51)=4.35\%\). That gap is diversification. With correlation 1 there would be no gap: the sd would be exactly 4.35%. With correlation 0 the covariance term disappears and the sd falls to 3.11%.


See it move
In the Portfolio Lab, load Tortoise & Hare and keep the weight at 0.5. Predict first: \(Var(P)\) with correlation 0, and with correlation \(-1\). (Correlation \(-1\) gives \(Cov=-1\times 0.5\times 1.5=-0.75\), the covariance in Worked example 4.2.) Move the correlation slider to check both, then press Go to min variance and see what weight the lab puts on the Tortoise. (Answers: 0.625 and 0.25.)


Your turn
Problem 4.1 (two drilling strategies, book Chapter 1). An oil company estimates a 20% chance of a small amount of oil, 50% of a moderate amount, and 30% of a large amount. Payoffs in millions of dollars:




Small
Moderate
Large




Standard drilling
20
30
40


Horizontal drilling
\(-20\)
40
80




Find the mean and variance of the payoff for each strategy.
Which strategy maximizes the expected payoff? Which would a risk-averse company choose, and why?
A geological survey would reveal the amount of oil before the company chooses. How much is that information worth?







TipSolution






Standard: \(E=0.2(20)+0.5(30)+0.3(40)=31\); \(E(X^2)=0.2(400)+0.5(900)+0.3(1600)=1010\); \(Var=1010-31^2=49\), sd 7. Horizontal: \(E=0.2(-20)+0.5(40)+0.3(80)=40\); \(E(X^2)=0.2(400)+0.5(1600)+0.3(6400)=2800\); \(Var=2800-1600=1200\), sd 34.6.
Horizontal has the higher mean, 40 against 31, but a far larger spread, including a loss in the small-oil case. A risk-averse company may give up 9 million in expected payoff for the much smaller variance of standard drilling.
With perfect information the company picks the better strategy in each state: 20, 40, 80, so the expected payoff is \(0.2(20)+0.5(40)+0.3(80)=48\). The best it can do without the information is 40. The survey is worth \(48-40=8\) million.




Problem 4.2 (diversifying with zero correlation, book Chapter 1). Investment \(X\) has mean return 5% and standard deviation 5%. Investment \(Y\) has mean 10% and standard deviation 6%. Their correlation is zero.

For the portfolio \(0.5X+0.5Y\), compute the mean and the variance. Is there a portfolio with a higher mean and a lower variance than \(X\)?
Suppose the correlation is 0.9 instead. Recompute the variance of \(0.5X+0.5Y\). Does the portfolio still beat \(X\) on both counts?







TipSolution






Mean \(0.5(5\%)+0.5(10\%)=7.5\%\). Variance \(0.25(0.05^2)+0.25(0.06^2)=0.000625+0.0009=0.001525\), below \(Var(X)=0.0025\). Yes: this portfolio has a higher mean and a lower variance than \(X\).
Add the covariance term \(2(0.5)(0.5)(0.9)(0.05)(0.06)=0.00135\): the variance is \(0.002875\), now above \(0.0025\). The portfolio still has the higher mean but no longer the lower variance, so the choice depends on how much risk you will take for the extra return. How much diversification helps depends on the correlation: the lower it is, the more of the noise cancels. Even at 0.9 the portfolio’s standard deviation, 5.36%, is below the weighted average of the two, 5.5%, but the gain is too small to beat \(X\).




Problem 4.3 (quick rules). True or false, with a one-line reason.

LeBron James makes 85% of his free throws and 50% of his field goals. In a game he takes 20 field goals (2 points each) and 10 free throws (1 point each). His expected score is 28.5 points, even if his shots are not independent.
If \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent with \(Var(X)=Var(Y)=6\), then \(Var(X+Y)=Var(2X)\).
If the correlation between \(X\) and \(Y\) is \(-0.81\) and their standard deviations are 20 and 25, then \(Cov(X,Y)=-405\).
If \(X\) takes the values 0, 1, 2 with equal probability, then its mean and variance are both 1.
A firm can spend $5,000 on a proposal and win an $80,000 contract with probability 0.5, or spend $10,000 and win with probability 0.6. To maximize expected value it should spend $10,000.







TipSolution






TRUE. \(2(20)(0.5)+1(10)(0.85)=20+8.5=28.5\), and linearity of expectation does not need independence.
FALSE. \(Var(X+Y)=6+6=12\), but \(Var(2X)=4(6)=24\). Two independent draws partly cancel; one draw doubled does not.
TRUE. \(Cov=r\,s_X s_Y=-0.81(20)(25)=-405\).
FALSE. The mean is 1, but \(Var=\tfrac13(0-1)^2+\tfrac13(0)^2+\tfrac13(2-1)^2=2/3\).
TRUE. \(0.5(80{,}000)-5{,}000=35{,}000\) against \(0.6(80{,}000)-10{,}000=38{,}000\).






Traps

Forgetting to square the constants: \(Var(2X)=4\,Var(X)\), not \(2\,Var(X)\).
Subtracting variances: \(Var(X-Y)=Var(X)+Var(Y)-2Cov(X,Y)\).
Mixing up variance and standard deviation. Variance is in squared units; quote the standard deviation when you interpret.
Dropping the covariance term from a portfolio variance.

title: AII 600 midterm study guide
text:
5. The binomial distribution

The idea
A Bernoulli trial has two outcomes, success (\(X=1\)) with probability \(p\) and failure (\(X=0\)). Its mean is \(p\) and, because \(X^2=X\), its variance is \(p-p^2=p(1-p)\). The variance is largest at \(p=1/2\): a fair coin is the noisiest yes/no question, and at \(p=0\) or \(p=1\) there is nothing left to learn.
A binomial random variable counts the successes in \(n\) Bernoulli trials. The conditions from class:

A fixed number of trials \(n\).
Each trial is a success or a failure.
The probability of success \(p\) is the same on every trial.
The trials are independent.

Then \(X\sim\text{Binomial}(n,p)\) and \[P(X=x)=\binom{n}{x}p^x(1-p)^{n-x}, \qquad \binom{n}{x}=\frac{n!}{x!\,(n-x)!}.\] Each particular sequence with \(x\) successes has probability \(p^x(1-p)^{n-x}\), and \(\binom{n}{x}\) counts how many such sequences there are.
Because \(X\) is a sum of \(n\) independent Bernoulli trials, Section 4 gives the mean and variance at once: means add, and for independent trials variances add. \[E(X)=np, \qquad Var(X)=np(1-p), \qquad sd(X)=\sqrt{np(1-p)}.\] The proportion of successes \(\hat p=X/n\) has mean \(p\) and standard deviation \(\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}\). Four times as many trials halve that standard deviation.
When it is not binomial. No fixed \(n\) (calls to 911 overnight: a count in a window, which is Poisson). A \(p\) that changes from trial to trial. Trials that are not independent: cards drawn without replacement, a hitter who runs hot and cold, loans that default together in a recession.


Recipe

Check the four conditions and write \(X\sim\text{Binomial}(n,p)\), saying what a success is.
Translate the event into values of \(X\). “More than 2” is \(\{3,4,\dots\}\); “at least 2” is \(\{2,3,\dots\}\); “at least one” is \(1-P(X=0)=1-(1-p)^n\).
Compute each term with the formula and add. If the complement has fewer terms, use it.
Compute \(np\) and \(\sqrt{np(1-p)}\). Say how many standard deviations the observed count is from \(np\).
Interpret, and say which condition would fail first in the real setting.



Worked example 5.1: DiMaggio’s hits in a game (class)
Joe DiMaggio hit 0.325. Treat his four at-bats in a game as independent trials with \(p=0.325\), so the number of hits is \(X\sim\text{Binomial}(4,0.325)\).

For example, \(P(X=2)=6(0.325)^2(0.675)^2=6(0.1056)(0.4556)=0.2888\).

More than two hits: \(P(X>2)=P(X=3)+P(X=4)=0.0927+0.0112=0.104\), or from the CDF, \(1-F(2)=1-0.8962=0.104\).
At least one hit: \(1-P(X=0)=1-0.675^4=0.7924\).
Mean \(np=4(0.325)=1.3\) hits; standard deviation \(\sqrt{4(0.325)(0.675)}=0.937\).

What it means: a three-hit game happens about one game in ten. The 56-game streak needs at least one hit in each of 56 games: \(0.7924^{56}=2.2\times 10^{-6}\), about 1 in 456,000, if games are independent. Hot and cold spells would make the streak more likely than this calculation says.


Worked example 5.2: the Patriots’ coin tosses (class)
The Patriots won 19 of 25 coin tosses in the 2014 to 2015 season. With a fair coin, the number of wins is \(Y\sim\text{Binomial}(25,\tfrac12)\).

Exactly 19: \(\binom{25}{19}0.5^{25}=177{,}100/33{,}554{,}432=0.0053\).
At least 19, the more honest question: add the terms for 19 through 25. The counts are \(177{,}100+53{,}130+12{,}650+2{,}300+300+25+1=245{,}506\), so \(P(Y\ge 19)=245{,}506/33{,}554{,}432=0.0073\).
Mean \(12.5\), standard deviation \(\sqrt{25(0.5)(0.5)}=2.5\). Nineteen is \((19-12.5)/2.5=2.6\) standard deviations above the mean.

What it means, and what it does not: a fair coin rarely gives one team 19 or more wins. But the league has 32 teams. The chance that at least one of them does this in a season is \(1-(1-0.0073)^{32}=0.21\). Rare for one team chosen in advance is not rare for somebody in the league. And \(P(\text{data}\mid\text{fair})\) small is not \(P(\text{fair}\mid\text{data})\) small: to get that you need a prior on cheating, exactly as in Section 3.


Worked example 5.3: one click and a hundred clicks (class)
A headline converts each visitor with probability \(p=0.6\), independently.

One visitor is a Bernoulli trial with standard deviation \(\sqrt{0.6\times 0.4}=0.49\). Whether the next visitor clicks is close to a coin flip.
The proportion who click among 100 visitors has standard deviation \(\sqrt{0.6\times 0.4/100}=0.049\). Among 400 visitors, \(0.0245\).

What it means: more data makes the estimate of \(p\) precise; it never makes the next click predictable. These are the two standard deviations in the class slide, and they answer different questions.


Worked example 5.4: guessing on a true/false quiz, by hand
A student guesses on 5 true/false questions, so the number of right answers is \(X\sim\text{Binomial}(5,\tfrac12)\). With \(p=\tfrac12\) every sequence of right and wrong answers has the same probability, \((\tfrac12)^5=\tfrac{1}{32}\), so \(P(X=x)=\binom5x/32\) and no calculator is needed.

At least 4 right: \(P(X\ge 4)=1-F(3)=6/32=3/16\approx 0.19\).

A scoring rule. Suppose a right answer earns 1 point and a wrong answer costs 1 point. One guess is worth \(\tfrac12(1)+\tfrac12(-1)=0\) on average, so the expected score is 0 however many questions you guess on. Expected values add, so this needs no independence.

What it means: about one blind guesser in five gets at least 4 of 5 right, so a good score on a short quiz is weak evidence of knowledge. The penalty makes blind guessing worthless on average. Partial knowledge changes that, as Problem 5.6 shows.


See it move
In the Galton Board Lab, each ball bounces right or left at every row of pegs, and its bin counts the right bounces: a binomial count. Set the rows of pegs to 4 and the chance of bouncing right to 0.3, a .300 hitter’s four at-bats. Predict first: the share of balls in bin 0, and the mean and standard deviation of the bin. Turn on the exact expected counts, drop 1,000 balls, and compare. (Answers: \(0.7^4=0.24\); mean 1.2; standard deviation \(\sqrt{0.84}\approx 0.92\).) Then open the Streaks Lab in Coin tosses mode, which starts with the Patriots’ numbers. Predict from Worked example 5.2 how often at least one of 32 teams wins 19 or more of 25 tosses, then run 1,000 seasons. (About 21% of seasons.)


Your turn
Problem 5.1 (the World Series, book Chapter 1). In 2006 the St. Louis Cardinals led the World Series 3 games to 1. The first team to win four games wins the series. Games are independent.

If the Cardinals win each game with probability 0.55, what is the probability that they win the series?
In 2012 the Cardinals led another series 3 games to 1, but now with probability 0.45 of winning each game. What is the probability that they win?
The series stops as soon as one team has four wins, so the number of games is not fixed. Why can you still answer as if all three remaining games were played?
Which assumption is the weakest here?







TipSolution






The Cardinals lose the series only if they lose all three remaining games: \(1-0.45^3=1-0.091=0.909\).
\(1-0.55^3=1-0.166=0.834\). A 3 to 1 lead is worth a lot even for the weaker team.
Imagine the remaining three games are played no matter what. The Cardinals win the series exactly when they win at least one of the three, so the probability is the same. The games after the decision do not change who won.
Independence and a constant \(p\). Starting pitchers rotate, home field changes, and a team down 1 to 3 may change its lineup.




Problem 5.2 (defective chips, book Chapter 1). Historically, 15% of the chips a company makes are defective. A quality check takes a random sample of 10 chips.

What is the probability that exactly one chip is defective?
That none is defective?
That at least two are defective?
Find the mean and standard deviation of the number of defective chips.
One morning the sample has 5 defective chips. How many standard deviations above the mean is that? \(P(X\ge 5)=0.0099\). What would you conclude, and what would you check?







TipSolution






\(\binom{10}{1}(0.15)(0.85)^9=10(0.15)(0.2316)=0.347\). Not 0.15: there are ten places the defect could be.
\(0.85^{10}=0.197\).
\(1-P(0)-P(1)=1-0.197-0.347=0.456\).
Mean \(10(0.15)=1.5\); standard deviation \(\sqrt{10(0.15)(0.85)}=\sqrt{1.275}=1.13\).
\((5-1.5)/1.13=3.1\) standard deviations. If the defect rate were still 15%, a sample this bad would happen about once in 100 mornings. More likely something changed: check the production line, and check whether the 10 chips really were a random sample rather than chips from one bad batch, which would break independence.




Problem 5.3 (quick checks, book Chapter 1). True or false, with a reason.

A mortgage bank knows that 2% of its loans default. If it makes 10 loans, the probability that at least one defaults is 95%.
40% of an amateur bowler’s throws are gutter balls. In 90 throws, the number of gutter balls has mean 36 and standard deviation 3.65.
The number of emails you receive in an hour is a binomial random variable.
You deal 5 cards from a shuffled deck. The number of aces is \(\text{Binomial}(5,\tfrac{1}{13})\).
For a Bernoulli trial, \(p=0.5\) gives the largest variance.







TipSolution






FALSE. \(1-0.98^{10}=0.183\). And loans default together in a recession, so independence is doubtful, which changes the answer further.
FALSE. The mean is \(90(0.4)=36\), but the standard deviation is \(\sqrt{90(0.4)(0.6)}=\sqrt{21.6}=4.65\).
FALSE. There is no fixed number of trials. It is a count in a time window, which is what the Poisson distribution models.
FALSE. The cards are drawn without replacement, so the probability that the next card is an ace changes with what has been dealt. The trials are not independent.
TRUE. \(p(1-p)\) is largest at \(p=1/2\), where it equals \(1/4\).




Problem 5.4 (Floyd Landis, book Chapter 2). Floyd Landis was disqualified after winning the 2006 Tour de France because a doping test came back positive. As a race leader he gave 8 samples, so there were 8 chances for a false positive.

Suppose the test has specificity 95%, and Landis is clean. Assume the 8 tests are independent. What is the probability that all 8 are negative? That at least one is a false positive?
Repeat (a) with specificity 99%.
How would you use Bayes rule to assess the probability that Landis doped? What else do you need?







TipSolution






\(0.95^8=0.663\), so the chance of at least one false positive is \(1-0.663=0.337\). A clean rider who is tested 8 times has about a one in three chance of a positive.
\(0.99^8=0.923\), so \(1-0.923=0.077\).
You need a prior, the share of riders like Landis who dope, and the probability that a doping rider tests positive. Then combine them with the evidence actually observed (one positive among 8 samples, not “a positive”) in Bayes rule. Testing a clean rider many times makes a false positive likely, so a single positive is weaker evidence than it sounds.




Problem 5.5 (the closer, class). You hired a closer. Half the people from this bootcamp convert 70% of qualified leads; the other half convert 30%. In the first week, the new closer converts 3 of 4 leads. Treat the leads as independent.

Compute the likelihood ratio \(P(\text{3 of 4}\mid 70\%)/P(\text{3 of 4}\mid 30\%)\). Why do the binomial coefficients not matter?
Find \(P(\text{70\% closer}\mid\text{3 of 4})\).
Repeat (b) for 4 of 4, and for 2 of 4.







TipSolution






\(\dfrac{\binom43 0.7^3(0.3)}{\binom43 0.3^3(0.7)}=\dfrac{0.1029}{0.0189}=5.44\). The coefficient \(\binom43=4\) is the same under both hypotheses, so it cancels.
Prior odds are 1, so the posterior odds are 5.44 and the probability is \(5.44/6.44=0.845\). Four leads moved you from 50% to 85%. Four leads is a small sample, but not too small to learn from: Bayes rule already accounts for the size.
4 of 4: likelihood ratio \((0.7/0.3)^4=29.6\), probability \(29.6/30.6=0.967\). 2 of 4: likelihood ratio \(\dfrac{0.7^2 0.3^2}{0.3^2 0.7^2}=1\), so the probability stays at 0.5. Two of four is exactly as likely under either kind of closer, so it tells you nothing.




Problem 5.6 (a three-option quiz, by hand). A quiz has 3 questions, each with 3 options, exactly one of them correct. A student guesses at random on every question. Let \(X\) be the number of correct answers.

Name the distribution of \(X\) and check the conditions.
Make a table of \(P(X=x)\) and \(F(x)\). Use fractions.
What is the probability of at least 2 correct answers?
Find \(E(X)\) and \(sd(X)\).
A correct answer earns 1 point and a wrong answer costs \(1/2\) point. What is the expected score of a student who guesses on every question? A second student can rule out one wrong option on every question and guesses between the other two. What is that student’s expected score?







TipSolution






\(X\sim\text{Binomial}(3,\tfrac13)\). There is a fixed number of trials, \(n=3\); each answer is right or wrong; \(p=\tfrac13\) on every question because the pick is random; and picks on different questions are independent.
\(P(X=x)=\binom3x(\tfrac13)^x(\tfrac23)^{3-x}=\binom3x 2^{3-x}/27\).



\(x\)

\(P(X=x)\)
8/27

6/27
1/27


\(F(x)\)
8/27
20/27

1



\(P(X\ge 2)=(6+1)/27=7/27\approx 0.26\), or \(1-F(1)=1-20/27\).
\(E(X)=3(\tfrac13)=1\). \(Var(X)=3(\tfrac13)(\tfrac23)=\tfrac23\), so \(sd(X)=\sqrt{2/3}\approx 0.82\) (check: \(0.82^2\approx 0.67\)).
One random guess is worth \(\tfrac13(1)+\tfrac23(-\tfrac12)=\tfrac13-\tfrac13=0\), so the expected score is \(3\times 0=0\). With one wrong option ruled out, \(p=\tfrac12\) and one guess is worth \(\tfrac12(1)+\tfrac12(-\tfrac12)=\tfrac14\), so the expected score is \(\tfrac34\). The penalty of \(\tfrac12\) is set so that blind guessing is worth nothing; any partial knowledge makes guessing pay on average.






Traps

Forgetting \(\binom{n}{x}\): “exactly one defective in 10” has ten possible positions.
Mixing up “more than” and “at least”.
Writing the standard deviation as \(np(1-p)\). That is the variance; take the square root.
Using the binomial when the trials are dependent or \(p\) changes. Say which condition you are assuming.

title: AII 600 midterm study guide
text:
6. The normal distribution

The idea
For a continuous random variable, probabilities are areas under a density curve. Any single exact value has probability zero, so \(P(X<a)\) and \(P(X\le a)\) are the same.
The normal distribution \(X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)\) is the bell curve, centered at its mean \(\mu\), with spread set by the standard deviation \(\sigma\). The second number in \(N(\mu,\sigma^2)\) is the variance: \(N(190,100)\) has standard deviation 10, not 100. Class wrote the crash model as \(N(0.012,\,0.043^2)\) to make this explicit.
All normals are the same bell, shifted and stretched. Standardizing turns any normal into the standard normal \(Z\sim N(0,1)\): \[Z=\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma}.\] A \(z\)-value counts how many standard deviations \(x\) is from the mean. The area to the left of \(z\) is written \(\Phi(z)=P(Z\le z)\); software computes it (pnorm in R).
The one fact you need. The exam restates this fact wherever you need it: \[P(-1.96\le Z\le 1.96)=0.95.\] Together with the symmetry of the bell, it gives everything else the exam asks for.

Two tails of 2.5%. The 5% outside \(\pm 1.96\) splits equally: \(P(Z>1.96)=P(Z<-1.96)=0.025\).
Half on each side. \(P(Z<0)=P(Z>0)=0.5\), so half of any normal lies below its mean.
Ranges and guarantees. The middle 95% of \(X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)\) is \(\mu\pm 1.96\sigma\). The level that \(X\) exceeds only 2.5% of the time is \(\mu+1.96\sigma\), and the level it falls below only 2.5% of the time is \(\mu-1.96\sigma\).
Comparing without computing. The farther a cutoff is from the mean in standard deviations, the less probability lies beyond it. So you can rank two tail probabilities by their \(z\)-values alone: \(P(Z>1.5)<P(Z>1.33)\).
Bounding. If \(z>1.96\), then \(P(Z>z)<0.025\). If \(0<z<1.96\), then \(P(Z>z)\) is between 0.025 and 0.5.

In class you also met \(P(-1\le Z\le 1)\approx 0.68\). It is worth knowing, but the exam does not need it.
Linear changes and sums. If \(X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), then \(aX+b\sim N(a\mu+b,\ a^2\sigma^2)\). A sum of independent normals is normal, with the means added and the variances added.
The central limit theorem. The sum (or the average) of many independent draws is approximately normal, even when a single draw is not. For \(n\) independent draws with mean \(\mu\) and standard deviation \(\sigma\), the sum is approximately \(N(n\mu,\ n\sigma^2)\) and the average is approximately \(N(\mu,\ \sigma^2/n)\). The mean of the sum grows like \(n\), but its standard deviation only like \(\sqrt n\). The theorem needs independence: in the class Galton board with one coin per ball, it fails.
When the model is wrong. A \(z\) of \(-5\) is far beyond \(-1.96\); under the normal model its probability is below one in a million. When it happens anyway, the likelier conclusion is that the tails of the real distribution are heavier than normal.


Recipe

Write \(X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)\). If you were given a variance, take its square root now.
Sketch the bell. Mark \(\mu\), the points \(\mu\pm 1.96\sigma\), and the cutoff. Shade the area the question asks about.
Standardize: \(z=(x-\mu)/\sigma\). Below the mean, \(z\) is negative.
Place \(z\). At 0 the tail beyond it is 50%. Beyond \(\pm 1.96\) the tail is under 2.5%. In between, the tail is between 2.5% and 50%.
To compare two options, compare their \(z\)-values instead of computing probabilities.
For a range or a guarantee, work backward from 1.96: \(\mu\pm 1.96\sigma\), or \(\mu+1.96\sigma\) for the level exceeded only 2.5% of the time.
Interpret in the units of the problem, and say which parameter would have to change to change the decision.



Worked example 6.1: body weight (book Chapter 1)
Model weight as \(X\sim N(190,100)\) in pounds.

The variance is 100, so \(\sigma=10\).
The middle 95% of weights is \(190\pm 1.96(10)=190\pm 19.6\), from 170.4 to 209.6 pounds.
So 2.5% of people weigh more than 209.6 pounds, and 50% weigh less than 190.
Is 200 pounds unusual? \(z=(200-190)/10=1\), inside \(\pm 1.96\), so no: more than 2.5% of people weigh more than 200 pounds. (Software: 15.9%.)

The trap: using 100 as the standard deviation gives a “95% range” of \(190\pm 196\), from \(-6\) to 386 pounds. A negative weight is the alarm that you used the variance.


Worked example 6.2: test scores, a range and a percentile
Scores on a test are \(N(1000,\ 200^2)\).

The middle 95%: \(1000\pm 1.96(200)=1000\pm 392\), from 608 to 1392.
The score that beats 97.5% of test takers: 1392.
Between 608 and 1000: half of the middle 95%, so 47.5%.
Is 1300 in the top 2.5%? \(z=(1300-1000)/200=1.5<1.96\), so no: more than 2.5% of scores are above 1300.



Worked example 6.3: how extreme was the 1987 crash? (class)
Before October 1987, monthly S&P 500 returns were modeled as \(N(0.012,\ 0.043^2)\): a mean of 1.2% and a standard deviation of 4.3%. The October return was \(-21.76\%\).
\(z=(-0.2176-0.012)/0.043=-5.34\). That is far beyond \(-1.96\), so under the model a month this bad has probability far below 2.5%. Software puts it at \(4.7\times 10^{-8}\): one month in about 21 million, or once in 1.8 million years.
What it means: either we saw a once-in-a-million-years event, or the normal model understates the tails of stock returns. The class histogram of S&P returns against the fitted normal settles it: real returns have far more extreme months than the bell allows. A model fitted to calm months is not safe to use for risk.


Worked example 6.4: is a 70% click rate surprising? (class, the central limit theorem)
The headline from Worked example 5.3 has true rate \(p=0.6\). Among 100 visitors, would an observed rate of 70% be surprising?
The observed rate \(\hat p\) is an average of 100 independent clicks, so by the central limit theorem it is approximately \(N(0.6,\ 0.049^2)\). Then \(z=(0.70-0.60)/0.049=2.04\), beyond 1.96, so a rate this high happens less than 2.5% of the time. (Software: 2.1%.)
What it means: a 70% rate from 100 visitors would be unusual if the truth were 60%. With only 25 visitors the standard deviation would be 0.098, \(z\) would be about 1, well inside \(\pm 1.96\), and 70% would be unremarkable. The same observed rate means more when it rests on more data.


See it move
In the Normal Tails Lab, set the mean to 0 and the SD to 1, choose \(a<X<b\), and set \(a=-1.96\) and \(b=1.96\): the shaded area is 0.95. Switch to \(X>b\) and read 0.025. Predict first, then check: with mean 190 and SD 10 (Worked example 6.1), the probability above 209.6 pounds, and the probability above 200 pounds. Then load the 1987 crash case, predict its \(z\) from Worked example 6.3, and turn on Compare with Student-t to see how much a fat tail changes the answer. For the central limit theorem, the Sampling Distribution Lab draws averages from a population you choose: pick a skewed one, predict what happens to the spread of the averages when the sample size is multiplied by 4, then draw 1,000 samples. (Answers: 0.025; 0.159; \(z=-5.34\); the spread halves.)


Your turn
Problem 6.1 (choosing a filling machine). Cereal boxes are labeled 500 grams, and a box that holds less than 500 grams is underfilled. Machine A fills \(N(510,\ 4^2)\) grams. Machine B fills \(N(515,\ 8^2)\) grams. Use only \(P(-1.96\le Z\le 1.96)=0.95\) and symmetry.

Compute the \(z\)-score of 500 grams for each machine. Which machine underfills less often? Is each machine’s underfill rate above or below 2.5%?
Machine B’s mean stays at 515. How small must its standard deviation be to match machine A’s underfill rate? How small to bring B’s underfill rate down to 2.5%?
A new rule counts a box as underfilled below 505 grams. Compare the machines again. What do you notice?
Under a rule of 510 grams, what share of machine A’s boxes is underfilled? Which machine is better? Explain in one sentence why the answer flips.
Machine A’s maker promises a fill that A’s boxes fall below only 2.5% of the time. What fill is that? A store checks 12 boxes from A. What is the probability that at least one falls below the promised fill? What did you assume?







TipSolution






A: \(z=(500-510)/4=-2.5\). B: \(z=(500-515)/8=-1.875\). A’s cutoff sits further out in its lower tail, so A underfills less often. A’s \(z\) is beyond \(-1.96\), so A underfills fewer than 2.5% of boxes; B’s \(z\) is inside, so B underfills more than 2.5%. (Software: 0.6% and 3.0%.) Choose A, even though B fills more on average.
Match the \(z\): \((500-515)/\sigma_B=-2.5\) gives \(\sigma_B=6\) grams. For a 2.5% rate: \((500-515)/\sigma_B=-1.96\) gives \(\sigma_B=15/1.96=7.65\) grams.
A: \(z=(505-510)/4=-1.25\). B: \(z=(505-515)/8=-1.25\). The same \(z\) means the same underfill rate: the machines tie at a 505 limit.
For A, 510 is the mean, so exactly 50% of its boxes are underfilled. For B, \(z=(510-515)/8=-0.625\), below the mean, so less than 50%: B is better. Far below both means, the wider spread of B puts more of its boxes in the tail; close to the means, B’s higher mean matters more. Which machine wins depends on where the limit sits relative to the means and spreads.
\(510-1.96(4)=502.16\) grams. Each box falls below it with probability 0.025, so \(P(\text{at least one of }12)=1-0.975^{12}=0.262\), assuming the boxes are independent. Boxes filled in the same run may share a problem, which would break that assumption.




Problem 6.2 (snowboards, book Chapter 1). Snowboard life is normal with mean 10 years and standard deviation 3 years. A board is defective if its life is less than 5 years.

Is the share of defective boards above or below 2.5%? Explain with a \(z\)-score.
The maker wants a warranty period that only 2.5% of boards fail to reach. How long should the warranty be?
With that warranty, let \(N\) be the number of warranty claims in a shipment of 120 boards. Name the distribution of \(N\), and find its mean and standard deviation. What is the probability of no claims?
One shipment produces 9 claims. How many standard deviations above the mean is that? Software gives \(P(N\ge 9)=0.003\) for this binomial. What would you conclude, and what would you check?







TipSolution






\(z=(5-10)/3=-1.67\), inside \(\pm 1.96\), so more than 2.5% of boards are defective. (Software: 4.8%.)
\(10-1.96(3)=4.12\) years. Only 2.5% of boards wear out before then.
\(N\sim\text{Binomial}(120,\ 0.025)\): mean \(120(0.025)=3\), standard deviation \(\sqrt{120(0.025)(0.975)}=1.71\). \(P(N=0)=0.975^{120}=0.048\).
\((9-3)/1.71=3.5\) standard deviations above the mean. If boards fail independently, each with probability 0.025, a shipment this bad happens about 3 times in 1,000. More likely something changed: check whether the shipment came from one bad production run, which would break independence, or whether the life model itself is off.




Problem 6.3 (Black Monday in China, book Chapter 1). On 24 August 2015, Chinese stocks fell 8.5% in one day. Over the previous 25 years, daily returns averaged 0.09% with a standard deviation of 2.6%, and 56% of days closed within one standard deviation of the mean. For the S&P 500 that share was 74%. Under a normal model, about 68% of days would fall within one standard deviation.

Compute the \(z\)-score of the 8.5% drop. Under a normal model, is a drop at least this large rarer than 2.5% of days?
Compare the normal model’s 68% with the 56% for China and the 74% for the S&P 500.
What do (a) and (b) say about the normal model for each market?







TipSolution






\(z=(-8.5-0.09)/2.6=-3.30\), far beyond \(-1.96\), so under the normal model a drop this large happens on far fewer than 2.5% of days. (Software: 0.0005, about one trading day in 2,100, roughly once in 8 years.) Notice that 25 years is about 6,300 trading days, so even the normal model expects about three such days in the sample. Rare on a given day is not rare over 25 years.
China has too few days near the mean (56% against 68%); the S&P 500 has too many (74%).
Neither market is normal, and China is further off. For the S&P 500, too many quiet days with the same standard deviation means that the rest of the variance must come from a few wild days: heavier tails than the bell. For China, only 56% of days near the mean says the bell shape itself is wrong, so a mean and a standard deviation do not describe a typical Chinese trading day. In both markets, a normal model fitted with the historical standard deviation misjudges how often extreme days happen.




Problem 6.4 (a hundred spins of roulette). You bet $1 on black 100 times at a European wheel. From Worked example 4.1, each bet has mean \(-0.027\) and standard deviation 1.00.

Use the central limit theorem to describe your total winnings \(S\) after 100 bets.
Give a range that contains \(S\) with probability about 95%. Is being ahead after 100 bets unusual?
Now play 10,000 bets. Repeat (a) and (b). What does the comparison teach about the house edge?







TipSolution






Mean \(100(-0.027)=-2.70\), standard deviation \(\sqrt{100}(1.00)=10.0\). So \(S\approx N(-2.70,\ 10^2)\).
\(-2.70\pm 1.96(10.0)=-2.70\pm 19.6\), from \(-\$22.30\) to \(\$16.90\). Zero is well inside the range, only 0.27 standard deviations above the mean, so being ahead after 100 bets is common. (Software: about 39%.)
Mean \(10{,}000(-0.027)=-270\), standard deviation \(\sqrt{10{,}000}(1.00)=100\). The 95% range is \(-270\pm 196\), from \(-\$466\) to \(-\$74\). Zero is above the whole range, so being ahead is rarer than 2.5%. (Software: 0.3%.) The expected loss grows like \(n\) and the spread only like \(\sqrt n\), so in the long run the edge swamps the luck. A short session is a gamble; a long one is a loss.




Problem 6.5 (earnings day, book Chapter 1). On an earnings announcement, a stock beats expectations 75% of the time. When it beats, its return is \(N(10\%,\ 5\%^2)\). When it misses, its return is \(N(-5\%,\ 8\%^2)\). Use the 1.96 fact and symmetry, and give bounds where you cannot give exact values.

What is the probability that the return is below \(-5\%\)?
What is the probability that the return is above 10%?







TipSolution






Total probability over the two cases. If the stock beats, \(z=(-5-10)/5=-3\), beyond \(-1.96\), so the chance is below 0.025. If it misses, \(-5\%\) is the mean, so the chance is exactly 0.5. The total is \(0.75\times(\text{less than }0.025)+0.25(0.5)\), between 0.125 and \(0.125+0.019=0.144\). Almost all of it comes from the misses. (Software: 0.126.)
If it beats, 10% is the mean, so the chance is 0.5. If it misses, \(z=(10+5)/8=1.875\), just inside 1.96, so the chance is a little more than 0.025. The total is \(0.75(0.5)+0.25\times(\text{a little more than }0.025)\), about \(0.375+0.006=0.38\). (Software: 0.383.)




Problem 6.6 (quick checks, adapted from book Chapter 1). True or false, with a one-line reason.

Steaks advertised as 16 ounces have weights \(N(16,\ 2^2)\). About 2.5% of steaks weigh less than 12.08 ounces.
Spending per visit at a theme park is \(N(\$60,\ \$15^2)\). Half of visitors spend less than $60, and about 95% spend between $30.60 and $89.40.
The cost of a 30-second commercial is \(N(10{,}000,\ 1{,}000^2)\). The probability that a commercial costs between 9,000 and 10,000 is 50%.
A stock’s returns on earnings day are \(N(5\%,\ 5\%^2)\). The probability of losing money that day is below 2.5%.
If \(X\sim N(50,25)\), then about 95% of values of \(X\) lie between 40.2 and 59.8.
If \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent and both \(N(0,1)\), then about 95% of values of \(X+Y\) lie between \(-1.96\) and \(1.96\).
If \(X\sim N(3,9)\), then \(P(X>1)=0.254\).







TipSolution






TRUE. \(16-1.96(2)=12.08\) is the level that only 2.5% of steaks fall below.
TRUE. The mean splits the bell in half, and \(60\pm 1.96(15)=60\pm 29.4\).
FALSE. Half of all commercials cost less than 10,000, and part of that half costs less than 9,000. Since 9,000 is within \(1.96\) standard deviations of the mean, more than 2.5% lies below it, so the interval holds less than 47.5%. (Software: 34%.)
FALSE. \(z=(0-5)/5=-1\), inside \(\pm 1.96\), so the chance of a loss is more than 2.5%. (Software: 16%.)
TRUE. The variance is 25, so \(\sigma=5\) and \(50\pm 1.96(5)=50\pm 9.8\).
FALSE. Variances of independent variables add, so \(X+Y\sim N(0,2)\), with standard deviation \(\sqrt 2=1.41\). The middle 95% is \(\pm 1.96(1.41)=\pm 2.77\).
FALSE. The value 1 is below the mean 3, so more than half of the distribution lies above it: \(P(X>1)>0.5\). (Software: 0.75.)






Traps

Using the variance as the standard deviation. Check the units: \(\sigma\) has the units of \(X\). A 95% range with impossible values is a warning sign.
Putting all 5% in one tail. The 5% outside \(\mu\pm 1.96\sigma\) splits: 2.5% in each tail.
Dropping the sign of \(z\) for values below the mean.
Writing the standard deviation of a sum of \(n\) draws as \(n\sigma\). It is \(\sqrt n\,\sigma\).
Treating a 5-sigma event as a miracle instead of as evidence against the model.

title: AII 600 midterm study guide
text:
7. Least squares

The idea
Regression predicts a response \(y\) from a predictor \(x\) with a line, \(\hat y=a+bx\). The line is a conditional mean: the average of \(y\) among cases with that value of \(x\). In class, with two groups of houses, you reported 2 for a small house and 6 for a large one; the regression line does the same thing with living area in place of the two groups.
A residual is the vertical distance from a point to the line, in the units of \(y\): \[e_i=y_i-\hat y_i.\] A positive residual means the point is above the line: the observed value is larger than predicted.
Least squares chooses \(a\) and \(b\) to make the sum of squared residuals as small as possible: \[SSE(a,b)=\sum_i (y_i-a-bx_i)^2.\] In class we wrote the same objective as the loss \(J(a,b)=\frac{1}{2n}\sum_i(a+bx_i-y_i)^2\); the factor \(\frac{1}{2n}\) does not change which line wins. Squaring stops positive and negative errors from canceling, and it punishes a big miss much more than several small ones.
The minimizing line has a formula: \[\hat b=\frac{\sum_i (x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)}{\sum_i (x_i-\bar x)^2}, \qquad \hat a=\bar y-\hat b\,\bar x.\] Two consequences you can use as checks: the line passes through the point of means \((\bar x,\bar y)\), and the residuals sum to zero.
Reading the coefficients.

The slope \(\hat b\) is the difference in predicted \(y\) between two cases whose \(x\) differs by one unit. Its units are units of \(y\) per unit of \(x\). It describes how \(y\) and \(x\) go together across the cases in the data, not what would happen if you changed \(x\) for one case.
The intercept \(\hat a\) is the predicted \(y\) at \(x=0\). It means something only if \(x=0\) is inside the range of the data. Otherwise it is an extrapolation whose job is to pin down the line.

Predicting inside the range of the data is interpolation. Predicting far outside it is extrapolation: the data say nothing about whether the line continues.
Influence. Write \(S_{xx}=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2\). Because \(\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)\bar y=0\), the slope is \(\hat b=\sum_i (x_i-\bar x)\,y_i/S_{xx}\), a weighted sum of the responses with weights proportional to \(x_i-\bar x\). So raising one response \(y_i\) by \(\Delta\) changes the slope by \[\Delta\,\frac{x_i-\bar x}{S_{xx}}.\] A point far from \(\bar x\) is a long lever and can tilt the line. A point at \(\bar x\) cannot change the slope at all; it only lifts the whole line by \(\Delta/n\).
Predictions as a matrix product (class). Put a column of ones next to the column of \(x\) values to form the design matrix \(X\), and let \(\theta=(a,b)\). Then the vector of predictions is \(X\theta\): each row produces one prediction, and the column of ones supplies the intercept. If two columns of \(X\) are identical, only the sum of their coefficients matters, so the coefficients are not unique. The predictions, and the loss, still are.


Recipe: a line by hand

Compute \(\bar x\) and \(\bar y\).
Make a table with columns \(x-\bar x\), \(y-\bar y\), their product, and \((x-\bar x)^2\). The first two columns must each sum to zero.
\(\hat b=\) (sum of products) / (sum of squares). Then \(\hat a=\bar y-\hat b\,\bar x\).
Fitted values \(\hat y_i=\hat a+\hat b x_i\) and residuals \(e_i=y_i-\hat y_i\). Check that the residuals sum to zero.
\(SSE=\sum_i e_i^2\).
Interpret the slope and the intercept in one sentence each, in units. Flag any extrapolation.



Worked example 7.1: three points (class)
The class data are \((0,1)\), \((1,3)\), \((2,3)\), so \(\bar x=1\) and \(\bar y=7/3\).

\(\hat b=2/2=1\) and \(\hat a=7/3-1(1)=4/3\), so \(\hat y=4/3+x\). The fitted values are \(4/3,\ 7/3,\ 10/3\), the residuals are \(-1/3,\ 2/3,\ -1/3\) (they sum to zero), and \(SSE=1/9+4/9+1/9=2/3\).
The class candidate line \(\hat y=1+x\) passes exactly through two of the points. Its residuals are \(0,\ 1,\ 0\) and its \(SSE\) is 1. The least squares line misses all three points and still wins: \(2/3<1\). In terms of the class loss, \(J=SSE/(2n)\) is \(1/9\) against \(1/6\).


Worked example 7.2: one point moves the line
Same three points, with \(S_{xx}=2\).

Raise the last response by 3, to \((2,6)\). That point has \(x-\bar x=1\), so the slope rises by \(3(1)/2=1.5\), to \(\hat b=2.5\). The new mean of \(y\) is \(10/3\), so \(\hat a=10/3-2.5(1)=0.83\).
Instead raise the middle response by 3, to \((1,6)\). That point sits at \(\bar x\), so the slope does not move: \(\hat b=1\). The whole line lifts by \(3/3=1\): \(\hat a=4/3+1=2.33\).

The same change in one response has completely different effects. The point at the edge has leverage; the point in the middle has none. In class, raising the rightmost response by 15 visibly tilted the whole line.


Worked example 7.3: reading a fitted line, Saratoga houses (class)
For 1,728 house sales, \(\hat y=13.44+113.12x\), with \(x\) in thousands of square feet and \(y\) in thousands of dollars. Living areas run from 616 to 5,228 square feet.

Slope. Two houses that differ by 1,000 square feet differ in predicted price by $113,120, about $113 per square foot. This compares different houses. It does not promise that a 1,000 square foot addition would raise the price of a given house by $113,120.
Prediction. At 2,200 square feet: \(13.44+113.12(2.2)=262.3\), about $262,300.
Intercept. 13.44 is the predicted price of a house with no living area, about $13,000. No house in the data is smaller than 616 square feet, so this is an extrapolation that anchors the line, not the value of the land.



See it move
In the Least Squares Lab, load the Clean line data. Turn on Draw squared residuals and Show my line and its handles. Predict first: can any line you draw have a smaller SSE than the least squares line? Try, then press Snap to least squares. Next, turn on The point \((\bar x,\bar y)\) and drag the rightmost point straight up. Predict which way the slope moves, and whether the line still passes through \((\bar x,\bar y)\). Then drag a point near the middle by the same amount and compare, as in Worked example 7.2.


Your turn
Problem 7.1 (salary and experience). Five employees:



Experience \(x\) (years)
2
4
6

Salary \(y\) ($1,000s)
60
