Fit the least squares line by hand. Interpret the slope and the intercept in the units of the problem.
Compute the fitted values and the residuals. Check that the residuals sum to zero, and compute \(SSE\).
Predict the salary at 7 years and at 30 years. Which prediction do you trust, and why?
The 10-year employee’s salary is corrected from 88 to 98. Recompute \(\hat b\) and \(\hat a\). Then go back to the original data and suppose instead that the 6-year employee earns 84 rather than 74. Recompute. Explain the difference.







TipSolution






\(\bar x=6\) and \(\bar y=74\). The deviations are \(x-\bar x=-4,-2,0,2,4\) and \(y-\bar y=-14,-6,0,6,14\). Products: \(56,12,0,12,56\), sum 136. Squares: \(16,4,0,4,16\), sum 40. So \(\hat b=136/40=3.4\) and \(\hat a=74-3.4(6)=53.6\). Each extra year of experience goes with $3,400 more salary, on average. The intercept, $53,600, is the predicted salary with no experience; nobody in the data has less than 2 years, so it is a mild extrapolation.
Fitted values \(60.4,\ 67.2,\ 74.0,\ 80.8,\ 87.6\). Residuals \(-0.4,\ 0.8,\ 0,\ -0.8,\ 0.4\), which sum to zero. \(SSE=0.16+0.64+0+0.64+0.16=1.6\).
At 7 years: \(53.6+3.4(7)=77.4\), about $77,400. Seven is inside the data, so this is interpolation and is reasonable. At 30 years: \(53.6+3.4(30)=155.6\). Thirty is far outside 2 to 10 years. Salaries usually flatten with seniority, and five data points cannot say whether the line continues.
Changing \(y\) at \(x=10\) by \(\Delta=10\): the slope changes by \(10(10-6)/40=1\), so \(\hat b=4.4\). The new \(\bar y\) is 76, so \(\hat a=76-4.4(6)=49.6\). Changing \(y\) at \(x=6\) by 10: \(x-\bar x=0\), so \(\hat b=3.4\) is unchanged, and \(\hat a=76-3.4(6)=55.6\), a lift of \(10/5=2\). A point at the mean of \(x\) can only lift the line; a point at the edge tilts it.




Problem 7.2 (reading a fitted model). A regression of weekly sales (thousands of units) on advertising spend (thousands of dollars) over 30 weeks gave \(\hat y=4.20+0.35x\). Weekly ad spend ranged from $5,000 to $40,000.

Interpret the slope in the units of the problem.
Predict sales in a week with $20,000 of advertising.
Interpret the intercept. Should the marketing team report it as “the sales we would get with no advertising”?
The manager says: “At $20,000 we sell 11,200 units, so doubling the budget to $40,000 will double sales.” Check the claim against the model. Then give one reason, beyond the arithmetic, to doubt that the slope measures the effect of advertising.







TipSolution






Weeks with $1,000 more advertising sold 350 more units, on average.
\(4.20+0.35(20)=11.2\), about 11,200 units.
The model predicts 4,200 units with no advertising. But no week in the data spent less than $5,000, so zero is outside the data and the intercept is an extrapolation. It may be roughly right; the data cannot confirm it.
The model gives \(4.20+0.35(40)=18.2\) at $40,000, not \(2(11.2)=22.4\): doubling \(x\) does not double \(\hat y\) when the intercept is not zero. Beyond the arithmetic: the slope compares weeks, and weeks with big budgets may be holiday weeks, when sales are high anyway. Then the slope mixes the effect of advertising with the effect of the season.




Problem 7.3 (predictions as a matrix product, class). Let \[X=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\1&3\\1&5\end{pmatrix},\qquad \theta=\begin{pmatrix}10\\2\end{pmatrix}.\]

Compute \(X\theta\). What does each row of the result represent? Which column of \(X\) carries the intercept?
Add a third column to \(X\), identical to the second, so the model is \(\hat y=\theta_0+\theta_1x+\theta_2x\). Show that \(\theta=(10,2,0)\), \((10,0,2)\), and \((10,5,-3)\) give the same predictions. What can the fit still tell you, and what can it not?







TipSolution






\(X\theta=(10+2\cdot 2,\ 10+2\cdot 3,\ 10+2\cdot 5)=(14,\ 16,\ 20)\). Each entry is the prediction for one observation (one row of \(X\)). The column of ones carries the intercept.
The predictions depend only on \(\theta_1+\theta_2\), which is 2 in all three cases, so all three give \((14,16,20)\). The predictions and the loss are determined by the data; the separate coefficients are not. You cannot say how much of the effect belongs to each of two identical columns.






Traps

Mixing up \(\sum(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)\) and \(\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2\): the slope has the products on top.
Computing \(\hat a=\bar y-\hat b\,\bar y\). It is \(\bar x\) that goes with \(\hat b\).
Interpreting a slope as what would happen if you changed \(x\) for one case.
Treating the intercept as meaningful when \(x=0\) is outside the data.
Trusting predictions far outside the range of \(x\).

title: AII 600 midterm study guide
text:
8. Checking a regression

The idea
A fitted line is a model. In class we wrote it as \[Y_i\mid x_i\sim N(a+bx_i,\ \sigma^2),\quad\text{independently}.\] That one line makes four claims: the mean of \(y\) is a straight line in \(x\); the errors are normal; they have the same spread \(\sigma\) at every \(x\); and they are independent.
Least squares is maximum likelihood under this model. The log-likelihood is \[\ell(a,b)=-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_i (y_i-a-bx_i)^2+C,\] where \(C\) does not depend on \(a\) or \(b\). Maximizing \(\ell\) is the same as minimizing the sum of squares, so the least squares line is the maximum likelihood line when the errors are normal with constant variance. The normal density makes a large error extremely unlikely, so the fit will bend a lot to avoid one. That is why a single wild point can pull a least squares line: a residual of 10 costs 100 in the sum of squares, as much as a hundred residuals of 1.
The residual standard error \(\hat\sigma\) estimates \(\sigma\), the typical distance of a point from the line. Software reports it as “Residual standard error” and computes it as \(\sqrt{SSE/(n-2)}\); on the exam you will be given it. It turns the model into statements about individual cases:

About 95% of cases with a given \(x\) fall within \(\hat y\pm 1.96\,\hat\sigma\). (This ignores the uncertainty in the line itself, which is small when \(n\) is large.)
The standardized residual \(e_i/\hat\sigma\) counts how many \(\hat\sigma\) a case is from the line. Beyond about \(\pm 3\) is unusual under the normal model: look at that case.

Residual plots check the four claims. Plot the residuals, or the standardized residuals, against \(x\) (or against \(\hat y\)).








What you see
What it means
What to do




A random cloud around 0 with constant spread
The line is adequate
Nothing


A U shape or an inverted U
The mean curves; the line is wrong in a systematic way
Add a curved term such as \(x^2\)


One point far from all the others
An outlier
Check the record; refit with and without it; report both


Spread that grows with \(x\) (a fan)
The errors do not have one \(\sigma\); common with positive, skewed responses like money
Model \(\log y\)



Curvature and an outlier are different clues, and they have different remedies. An outlier far from \(\bar x\) is also influential: as in Section 7, it can tilt the line.


Recipe

Write the model, \(y\mid x\sim N(a+bx,\ \sigma^2)\), with \(\hat\sigma\) from the output.
For one case: compute \(\hat y\), the residual \(e=y-\hat y\), and the standardized residual \(e/\hat\sigma\). Beyond \(\pm 3\), investigate.
For a range of individual outcomes: \(\hat y\pm 1.96\,\hat\sigma\).
For a residual plot: look for shape (a curve), single points (outliers), and changing spread (a fan). Name the problem and one remedy.



Worked example 8.1: Saratoga, continued (class)
The Saratoga fit has \(\hat\sigma=69.10\), that is $69,100.

A 95% range at 2,200 square feet: \(262.3\pm 1.96(69.10)=262.3\pm 135.4\), from 126.9 to 397.7, so $127,000 to $398,000. The line pins down the average price of such houses, but individual houses vary a lot around it.
One unusual sale. A 2,200 square foot house sold for $500,000. Its residual is \(500-262.3=237.7\), so it sold $237,700 above the line. Its standardized residual is \(237.7/69.10=3.44\), which is unusual under the model. Check that the sale is recorded correctly, then ask what the house has that size does not capture: waterfront, land, condition. Do not delete it just because it is far from the line.



Worked example 8.2: Tiger Woods and the log scale (class)
In class we regressed the 2000 earnings of 195 golfers on four statistics: events played, driving distance, greens in regulation, and putts per round.

Dollar scale. Tiger Woods earned $9.19 million; the model predicts $3.58 million. His residual is $5.6 million, or \(e/\hat\sigma=8.3\) residual standard errors (\(\hat\sigma\approx\$0.67\) million). The class histogram puts him near 8.8, because R’s standardized residuals also adjust for how unusual a golfer’s statistics are. Under a normal model either number is essentially impossible. He alone contributes 37% of the sum of squared residuals, so one golfer shapes the whole fit.
Log scale. Regress \(\log(\text{earnings})\) on the same statistics. Tiger’s standardized residual becomes \(-0.57\) (\(e/\hat\sigma=-0.54\)): the log model predicts about $12.5 million for him, a bit more than he earned. The largest standardized residual on the log scale, 3.40, belongs to Notah Begay III.

What it means: on the dollar scale the model adds dollars for each statistic, and it cannot reach Tiger. On the log scale each statistic multiplies earnings, and Tiger’s exceptional statistics multiply into a large prediction. An outlier on one scale can be ordinary on another. The transformation changes which errors matter; it does not prove a causal story.


See it move
In the Regression Model Lab, every point is drawn from a normal distribution centered on the line, with the same spread \(\sigma\) at every \(x\). Turn on the \(\pm 2\sigma\) band. Predict first: what share of the points falls inside the band? Read Points within \(\pm 2\sigma\), then move the noise slider and watch the band and the points stretch together. Then in the Least Squares Lab, load Mammals on the raw scale and look at the residuals: a few giant animals dominate, and the spread fans out. Predict what a log-log scale will do, then load Mammals on the log-log scale. Worked example 8.2 is the same idea with golfers.


Your turn
Problem 8.1 (advertising, continued). For the advertising model of Problem 7.2, the residual standard error is 1.10 thousand units.

Give a range that should contain about 95% of weekly sales in weeks with $20,000 of advertising.
One such week sold 15,000 units. Compute its residual and standardized residual. What would you do about this week?
If the residual standard error were 3.0 instead, how would your answer to (b) change?







TipSolution






\(11.2\pm 1.96(1.10)=11.2\pm 2.16\), from 9.04 to 13.36: about 9,000 to 13,400 units.
\(e=15-11.2=3.8\) thousand units, and \(3.8/1.10=3.45\). Unusual under the model. Look for a cause: a holiday, a promotion, a competitor out of stock, or a data entry error. If there is a real reason, record it or model it; do not just delete the week.
Then \(3.8/3.0=1.27\), an ordinary week. Whether a residual is large depends on the typical scatter around the line.




Problem 8.2 (reading residual plots). Figure 1 shows standardized residuals from four straight-line fits. In all four, the response is a positive amount, such as weekly sales in dollars. For each panel, say whether the straight line is adequate. If not, name the problem and one remedy.








Figure 1: Standardized residuals plotted against x for four different fitted lines.











TipSolution






Panel 1. An inverted U: negative residuals at both ends, positive in the middle. The relationship bends downward, and the line overpredicts at both ends. Remedy: add an \(x^2\) term.
Panel 2. A random cloud around zero with constant spread, everything within \(\pm 3\). The line is adequate.
Panel 3. One point near \(-6\); the rest is random. An outlier far below the line. Check that record, refit without it to see how much the line moves, and report both fits.
Panel 4. A fan: the spread grows with \(x\). There is no single \(\sigma\), so \(\hat y\pm 1.96\hat\sigma\) is too wide at small \(x\) and too narrow at large \(x\). Remedy: model \(\log y\), which turns errors that grow in proportion to \(y\) into errors of constant size. The point near \(-3.7\) is part of the fan, not a separate outlier: with one \(\hat\sigma\) for every \(x\), residuals at large \(x\) look extreme because the spread there is larger. Fix the fan first, then look again.




Problem 8.3 (least squares and the normal model).

Write the log-likelihood for the model \(y_i\mid x_i\sim N(a+bx_i,\sigma^2)\), independently for \(i=1,\dots,n\). Show that maximizing it over \(a\) and \(b\) gives the least squares line.
Suppose the real errors have much heavier tails than the normal: wild errors are not rare. Would you still trust a line fitted by least squares? Why?
A colleague proposes to choose the line that minimizes the sum of the absolute residuals instead. Compared with least squares, how much would that line react to one wild point?







TipSolution






Each \(y_i\) has density \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma}\exp\left(-\frac{(y_i-a-bx_i)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)\). Independence makes the likelihood a product, so the log-likelihood is a sum: \[\ell(a,b)=-n\log\left(\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma\right)-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_i (y_i-a-bx_i)^2.\] The first term does not involve \(a\) or \(b\), and the second is \(-SSE/(2\sigma^2)\). Maximizing \(\ell\) means minimizing \(SSE\).
Less. Least squares is the right choice when large errors are rare, as under the normal. When wild errors are common, each one pulls the line hard, because its squared residual is huge. Look at the residual plots, and consider a transformation or a method less sensitive to outliers.
Much less. With absolute residuals, a residual of 10 costs 10, the same as ten residuals of 1, instead of 100. One wild point has far less pull. The price: this line is no longer the maximum likelihood line under normal errors.






Traps

Calling a point an outlier without computing its standardized residual.
Using \(\hat\sigma\) as if it were the uncertainty of the slope. It is the scatter of individual cases around the line.
Deleting an unusual case without checking it, or without reporting what the fit looks like with it.
Reading a U-shaped residual plot as “a few outliers”. A systematic pattern means the mean is wrong.

title: AII 600 midterm study guide
text:
9. Logistic regression

The idea
Many questions have a yes-or-no answer: will a customer cancel, is an email spam, will the favorite win. Code the answer as \(y=1\) for yes and \(y=0\) for no. The thing to predict is a probability, \(p=P(y=1\mid x)\). A straight line is the wrong tool for it: in class, a line through NBA wins and losses predicted values above 1 for large point spreads, and a probability has to stay between 0 and 1.
Logistic regression keeps the straight line but uses it on a different scale. It computes a linear score, which can be any number, \[z=\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\dots+\beta_px_p,\] and turns the score into a probability with the sigmoid (logistic) function \[p=\sigma(z)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}.\] The sigmoid is an S-curve. At \(z=0\) it gives \(p=0.5\); large positive scores give \(p\) near 1, large negative scores give \(p\) near 0, and \(p\) never leaves the interval from 0 to 1. It is symmetric about the middle, \(\sigma(-z)=1-\sigma(z)\), so the values for negative \(z\) follow from those for positive \(z\). These values are worth knowing (log is the natural logarithm):













\(z\)
\(-3\)
\(-2\)
\(-1\)
\(0\)
\(1\)
\(2\)
\(3\)




\(\sigma(z)\)
0.05
0.12
0.27
0.50
0.73
0.88
0.95


\(\log\sigma(z)\)
\(-3.0\)
\(-2.1\)
\(-1.3\)
\(-0.69\)
\(-0.31\)
\(-0.13\)
\(-0.05\)











Figure 2: Left: the sigmoid turns any score z into a probability; the dots are the table values. Right: the log loss of one prediction, for y = 1 and for y = 0.





Log-odds. Solving \(p=\sigma(z)\) for \(z\) gives \[z=\log\frac{p}{1-p}.\] The ratio \(p/(1-p)\) is the odds in favor of \(y=1\), so the score is the log-odds of \(y=1\). That is what the model makes linear: the log-odds are a straight line in \(x\), and the probability is an S-curve in \(x\) (Figure 2, left).
What a coefficient means. \(\beta_1\) is the change in the log-odds when \(x_1\) rises by one unit and the other predictors stay fixed. It is not a change in probability. How much \(p\) moves depends on where the case starts on the S-curve: one unit of \(z\) moves \(p\) from 0.50 to 0.73 in the middle, but only from 0.88 to 0.95 near the top. Equivalently, one more unit of \(x_1\) multiplies the odds by \(e^{\beta_1}\). Coefficients can be traded against each other on the log-odds scale. In the class LinkedIn model of who becomes an executive, one more job function had coefficient 0.26 and one more year of experience had 0.09, so one extra function was worth about three years of experience. And because the sigmoid is not linear, probability changes from separate predictors do not add: in class, six changes to person B, each worth 3 to 15 points on its own, took the probability from 15% to about 81%, not to the 52% that adding the separate lifts would give.
Log loss. Judge a probability by the probability it gave to what actually happened: \(p\) if \(y=1\), and \(1-p\) if \(y=0\). The log loss of one prediction is minus the log of that probability, \[J=-y\log p-(1-y)\log(1-p),\] which is \(-\log p\) when \(y=1\) and \(-\log(1-p)\) when \(y=0\) (Figure 2, right). A high probability for what happened costs almost nothing, and a confident mistake costs a lot. In class, two models predicted an event that did not happen, one with \(p=0.60\) and one with \(p=0.99\). The first lost \(-\log(0.40)=0.92\), the second \(-\log(0.01)=4.61\). A count of errors at a cutoff of 0.5 calls both of them one mistake; the log loss charges the model that was sure and wrong.
Log loss is maximum likelihood. For one observation, the probability of the observed outcome is \[P(Y=y\mid p)=p^y(1-p)^{1-y},\] which is \(p\) when \(y=1\) and \(1-p\) when \(y=0\). Its negative log is exactly the log loss. For independent observations the likelihood is a product, so the total log loss is minus the log-likelihood, and fitting the model by minimizing the total log loss is maximum likelihood. It is the same story as Section 8, where least squares is maximum likelihood under normal errors. Unlike least squares, there is no formula for the best coefficients: software climbs the log-likelihood in steps.


Recipe

Compute the score \(z=\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\dots\) for the case. Watch the signs and the 0/1 coding of yes-or-no predictors.
Turn the score into a probability, \(p=\sigma(z)\). For a negative score use \(\sigma(-z)=1-\sigma(z)\).
Interpret a coefficient on the log-odds scale: “one more unit of \(x\) raises the log-odds of \(y=1\) by \(\beta\), holding the other predictors fixed.” Never “raises the probability by \(\beta\).”
To trade two predictors, divide their coefficients: a coefficient of \(-2\) offsets four units of a predictor with coefficient 0.5.
For the log loss, find the probability the model gave to the outcome that happened, \(p\) if \(y=1\) and \(1-p\) if \(y=0\), and take minus its log.



Worked example 9.1: NBA point spreads (class)
The class model for the probability that the favorite wins an NBA game uses the point spread \(s\) and no intercept: \[\log\frac{p}{1-p}=0.156\,s.\]

Spread 0: \(z=0\) and \(p=0.50\). Without an intercept, a game with no favorite is a coin flip.
Spread 4: \(z=0.156(4)=0.62\) and \(p=\sigma(0.62)=0.65\).
Spread 8: \(z=1.25\) and \(p=0.78\).
Each extra point of spread adds 0.156 to the log-odds, which multiplies the odds of a win by \(e^{0.156}=1.17\).

What it means: doubling the spread from 4 to 8 does not double the probability, which goes from 0.65 to 0.78. The same step in log-odds buys less and less probability as the favorite gets stronger, and the probability never reaches 1. What would change it: the model has no intercept, so it says that a spread of 0 is exactly 50%. If home teams won more often than the spread says, an intercept would shift the whole curve.


Worked example 9.2: a hospital model by hand
A hospital models whether a patient is readmitted within 30 days of discharge (\(y=1\)) with \[z=-3+0.5\,\text{visits}+1\,\text{alone},\] where \(\text{visits}\) is the number of emergency room visits in the past year, and \(\text{alone}\) is 1 if the patient lives alone and 0 otherwise.

Probabilities. A patient with no visits who does not live alone has \(z=-3\) and \(p=0.05\). A patient with 4 visits who lives alone has \(z=-3+2+1=0\) and \(p=0.50\).
Coefficients. Each extra visit raises the log-odds of readmission by 0.5, holding living arrangements fixed. Living alone raises them by 1, as much as two extra visits.
Equal steps in \(z\), unequal steps in \(p\). For patients who live alone, going from 4 to 6 visits moves \(z\) from 0 to 1 and \(p\) from 0.50 to 0.73, up 0.23. Going from 8 to 10 visits moves \(z\) from 2 to 3 and \(p\) from 0.88 to 0.95, up only 0.07.
Log loss. A patient who lives alone with 8 visits (\(p=0.88\)) was not readmitted, so \(y=0\) and the loss is \(-\log(1-0.88)=-\log(0.12)=-\log\sigma(-2)=2.1\). A patient who lives alone with 4 visits (\(p=0.50\)) was readmitted: the loss is \(-\log(0.50)=0.69\). A patient with no visits who does not live alone (\(p=0.05\)) was readmitted: the loss is \(-\log(0.05)=3.0\).

What it means: the costliest prediction is the one that gave the outcome only a 5% chance. A prediction of 0.50 costs 0.69 whatever happens: it is the price of saying “I don’t know.” What would change it: the coefficients describe the patients in the hospital’s data. They say how readmission goes together with visits and living alone, not how one patient’s risk would change if that patient moved in with someone.


See it move
In the Logistic Regression Lab, the red S-curve is the class NBA model, \(\log\frac{p}{1-p}=0.156\times\text{spread}\). Predict first: the win probability at a spread of 0, and whether 4 more points of spread add more probability starting from a spread of 0 or from a spread of 12. Then use Predict at a spread to check 0, 4, 8, 12, and 16. Press New season a few times: the maximum likelihood fit to each simulated season lands near 0.156, but not on it. (Answers: 0.50; from 0, about 15 percentage points, against about 6 from 12.)


Your turn
Problem 9.1 (the sigmoid, book Chapter 13).

Show that \(\sigma(-z)=1-\sigma(z)\).
Use the table and part (a) to find \(\sigma(0)\), \(\sigma(2)\), and \(\sigma(-2)\).
The slope of the sigmoid is \(\sigma'(z)=\sigma(z)\big(1-\sigma(z)\big)\). Compute it at \(z=0\) and at \(z=2\). What does the difference say about how much a coefficient moves the probability?







TipSolution






\(\sigma(-z)=\dfrac{1}{1+e^{z}}\). Multiply the top and the bottom by \(e^{-z}\): \(\sigma(-z)=\dfrac{e^{-z}}{e^{-z}+1}\). And \(1-\sigma(z)=\dfrac{1+e^{-z}-1}{1+e^{-z}}=\dfrac{e^{-z}}{1+e^{-z}}\). The two are equal.
\(\sigma(0)=1/(1+1)=0.5\). \(\sigma(2)=0.88\) from the table, so \(\sigma(-2)=1-0.88=0.12\).
At \(z=0\): \(0.5\times 0.5=0.25\). At \(z=2\): \(0.88\times 0.12\approx 0.11\). Near the middle, a small change \(\Delta\) in the log-odds changes \(p\) by about \(0.25\,\Delta\), so a coefficient \(\beta\) moves \(p\) by about \(\beta/4\) per unit of \(x\). At \(z=2\) the same change moves \(p\) by less than half as much. In the NBA model, one more point of spread in an even game adds about \(0.156/4\approx 0.04\), four percentage points.




Problem 9.2 (accepting an offer). A university models whether an admitted student accepts its offer (\(y=1\)) with \[z=-2+1\,\text{visit}+0.5\,\text{aid},\] where \(\text{visit}\) is 1 if the student came to a campus visit day and \(\text{aid}\) is the scholarship in thousands of dollars.

Find the probability of accepting for a student with no visit and no aid, for a visitor with $2,000 of aid, and for a visitor with $4,000 of aid.
Interpret the coefficient on aid. How much aid is a campus visit worth on the log-odds scale?
A dean says: “Doubling a visitor’s aid from $2,000 to $4,000 doubles the chance that the student accepts.” Is the dean right?
For visitors, compare the effect of an extra $2,000 of aid on a student who already has $2,000 with its effect on a student who already has $6,000. Both add 1 to the log-odds. Why do they move the probability by different amounts?







TipSolution






No visit, no aid: \(z=-2\) and \(p=0.12\). Visitor with $2,000: \(z=-2+1+0.5(2)=0\) and \(p=0.50\). Visitor with $4,000: \(z=-2+1+2=1\) and \(p=0.73\).
Each extra $1,000 of aid raises the log-odds of accepting by 0.5, holding the visit fixed. A visit, with coefficient 1, is worth \(1/0.5=2\) units of aid, that is $2,000.
No. Going from $2,000 to $4,000 adds 1 to the log-odds, and the probability goes from 0.50 to 0.73, not to 1. A coefficient adds to the log-odds; it does not multiply the probability.
From $2,000 to $4,000, \(z\) goes from 0 to 1 and \(p\) from 0.50 to 0.73, up 0.23. From $6,000 to $8,000, \(z\) goes from 2 to 3 and \(p\) from 0.88 to 0.95, up 0.07. The S-curve is steep in the middle and flat near 1: a student who is already likely to accept has little room left to move.




Problem 9.3 (scoring a forecaster). A weather app gives the chance of rain each morning. On four days:



Day
1
2
3
4




Chance of rain \(p\)
0.88
0.88
0.50
0.05


Rained? \(y\)
1
0
1
1




Compute the log loss for each day, and the total.
Which day costs the most, and why?
A lazy app says 50% every day. What is its log loss each day, and its total over these four days? Which app scores better here, and what does that say about confidence?
Write the probability of one day’s outcome as a function of \(p\). Explain why the app with the smallest total log loss is the one under which the observed weather is most likely.







TipSolution






Day 1: \(y=1\), loss \(-\log 0.88=0.13\). Day 2: \(y=0\), loss \(-\log(1-0.88)=-\log 0.12=2.1\). Day 3: \(-\log 0.5=0.69\). Day 4: \(y=1\), loss \(-\log 0.05=3.0\). Total \(0.13+2.1+0.69+3.0=5.92\).
Day 4. The app gave rain a 5% chance and it rained: the most confident mistake costs the most. Day 2 is also a confident mistake, 88% for rain that did not come.
\(-\log 0.5=0.69\) every day, whatever happens, so the total is \(4\times 0.69=2.76\). The lazy app scores better on these four days, because the first app made two confident mistakes in four days. Confidence pays only when it is earned: an app that says 88% should see rain on about 88% of those days. Over many days, an informative app that is honest about its uncertainty beats the lazy one.
\(P(Y=y\mid p)=p^y(1-p)^{1-y}\). Treating the days as independent given the forecasts, the probability of the whole record is the product over days, and the total log loss is minus its log. The smallest total log loss is therefore the largest probability of the observed weather: maximum likelihood.




Problem 9.4 (true or false, book Chapter 13 and class). Answer TRUE or FALSE, with a one-sentence justification.

Logistic regression coefficients represent the change in probability for a one-unit increase in the predictor.
The odds ratio \(e^{\beta}\) for a predictor is always positive.
If the score is \(z=0\), the model’s probability is 0.5.
In the NBA model, doubling the spread doubles the probability that the favorite wins.
Two models predict \(p=0.60\) and \(p=0.99\) for an event that does not happen. Both are wrong at a cutoff of 0.5, so they receive the same log loss.
Minimizing the total log loss gives the maximum likelihood estimates of the coefficients.







TipSolution






FALSE. They are changes in the log-odds. The change in probability depends on where the case starts on the S-curve.
TRUE. \(e^{x}>0\) for every \(x\). A negative \(\beta\) gives an odds ratio between 0 and 1: the odds go down.
TRUE. \(\sigma(0)=1/(1+e^0)=1/2\).
FALSE. From a spread of 4 to 8 the probability goes from 0.65 to 0.78. The log-odds double; the probability does not.
FALSE. The losses are \(-\log 0.40=0.92\) and \(-\log 0.01=4.61\). The log loss charges the confident mistake more.
TRUE. The total log loss is minus the log-likelihood of independent Bernoulli outcomes, so minimizing one maximizes the other.






Traps

Reading a coefficient as a change in probability. It is a change in log-odds.
Using \(p\) in the log loss when \(y=0\). The loss uses the probability of what happened, \(1-p\).
Reading \(\sigma(-2)\) as 0.88. A negative score gives a probability below 0.5: \(\sigma(-2)=1-0.88=0.12\).
Adding probability changes from several predictors. Add on the log-odds scale, then convert once.
Forgetting that log is the natural logarithm.

title: AII 600 midterm study guide
text:
10. Concept check
Problem 10.1 (true or false). Answer TRUE or FALSE, with a one-sentence justification. On the exam the justification earns the point.

You roll two fair three-sided dice. The probability that they show the same number is 1/4.
If \(A\) and \(B\) are independent, \(P(A)>0\), and \(P(B)>0\), then \(P(A\text{ and }B)>0\).
If \(P(A\mid B)=0.5\) and \(P(B)=0.5\), then \(A\) and \(B\) are independent.
A box has three drawers: one holds two gold coins, one two silver coins, and one a gold and a silver coin. You pick a drawer at random and a coin from it at random, and the coin is gold. The probability that the drawer holds two gold coins is 50%.
45% of students play golf, 55% play tennis, and 70% play at least one of the two. Then 15% play golf but not tennis.
550 of 100,000 emails are spam. Half of all spam contains the word “bigger”, and 2% of other emails do. An email containing “bigger” is spam with probability about 12%.
Of 140 night club customers, 77 of the 91 under 30 are single and 28 of the 49 over 30 are single. Age and being single are independent.
If two random variables have nonzero correlation, they must be dependent.
If \(X\sim\text{Binomial}(10,\ 0.3)\), then \(Var(X)=3\).
The average of 400 independent measurements has one-twentieth the standard deviation of a single measurement.
A \(z\)-score of \(-2\) means the value is 2 units below the mean.
In a regression with an intercept, the least squares residuals sum to zero and the line passes through \((\bar x,\bar y)\).
In the Saratoga fit, the slope 113.12 means that adding 1,000 square feet to a house will raise its price by $113,120.
If two columns of the design matrix are identical, the least squares predictions are not unique.
In the Saratoga fit, a house with a standardized residual of 3.4 sold for $3,400 more than predicted.
Converting prices from thousands of dollars to dollars multiplies the slope, the intercept, and \(\hat\sigma\) by 1,000 and leaves the standardized residuals unchanged.
In a logistic regression, a coefficient of 0.5 means that one more unit of \(x\) raises the probability that \(y=1\) by 0.5.
A prediction of \(p=0.5\) has the same log loss whether \(y=0\) or \(y=1\).







TipSolution






FALSE. There are 9 equally likely pairs and 3 of them match: \(3/9=1/3\).
TRUE. \(P(A\text{ and }B)=P(A)P(B)>0\).
FALSE. Independence needs \(P(A\mid B)=P(A)\), and nothing says \(P(A)=0.5\).
FALSE. Of the three gold coins, two are in the gold-gold drawer, so the probability is \(2/3\). Bayes: \(\frac{1\cdot\frac13}{1\cdot\frac13+\frac12\cdot\frac13+0}=\frac23\).
TRUE. \(P(\text{both})=0.45+0.55-0.70=0.30\), so golf but not tennis is \(0.45-0.30=0.15\).
TRUE. \(\frac{0.5(0.0055)}{0.5(0.0055)+0.02(0.9945)}=\frac{0.00275}{0.02264}=0.121\).
FALSE. Among those under 30, \(77/91=0.85\) are single; among those over 30, \(28/49=0.57\).
TRUE. Independent variables have zero correlation, so nonzero correlation rules out independence.
FALSE. \(Var(X)=10(0.3)(0.7)=2.1\); 3 is the mean.
TRUE. \(\sigma/\sqrt{400}=\sigma/20\).
FALSE. It means 2 standard deviations below the mean.
TRUE. Both follow from the least squares formulas: \(\hat a=\bar y-\hat b\bar x\) puts \((\bar x,\bar y)\) on the line.
FALSE. The slope compares different houses in the data; it is not the effect of an addition to one house.
FALSE. The coefficients are not unique, but the predictions are.
FALSE. It sold 3.4 residual standard errors above the line: \(3.4\times\$69{,}100\), about $235,000.
TRUE. Every price, prediction, and residual is multiplied by 1,000, and the ratio \(e/\hat\sigma\) does not change.
FALSE. It raises the log-odds by 0.5. The change in probability depends on where the case starts on the S-curve, and it is never more than about \(0.5/4=0.125\).
TRUE. Either way the model gave the outcome probability 0.5, and the loss is \(-\log 0.5=0.69\).

title: AII 600 midterm study guide
text:
How to sit the exam

First five minutes. Read every problem. Start with the one you are surest about.
Budget. About 1.5 minutes per point. If a part takes twice its share, write down your setup and move on; come back at the end.
Set up before you compute. Name the events or the random variable, write the formula in symbols, then substitute numbers. Most partial credit is in the setup.
Arithmetic. There is no calculator. Write the formula in symbols, keep fractions as fractions, and cancel before you divide. A fraction such as \(3/8\) is a complete answer; for a decimal, two or three places are plenty. The next section shows the shortcuts.
Interpret. One sentence, in the units of the problem, about the people or things in the problem.
What would change. Name the assumption (independence, the prior, normality, a straight line, a constant \(p\)) and say which way the answer would move.
Normal problems. Standardize, then compare \(z\) with 0 and \(\pm 1.96\). When the 1.96 fact does not give an exact probability, the question is asking you to compare or bound instead.
Logistic problems. Compute the score \(z\) first, then read \(p\) from the table. For a negative score, or for \(1-p\), use \(\sigma(-z)=1-\sigma(z)\). Interpret a coefficient as a change in log-odds.
Sanity checks. Probabilities are between 0 and 1; a conditional distribution sums to 1; a variance is positive; residuals sum to zero; a shaded area smaller than half the bell gives a number below 0.5.
True or false. The justification earns the point. A one-line calculation or a counterexample is the best justification.

title: AII 600 midterm study guide
text:
Arithmetic without a calculator
The exam’s numbers are chosen so that every calculation is short. A few habits make hand arithmetic fast and safe.

Fractions first. Keep fractions until the end and cancel before you divide: \(0.42/0.45=42/45=14/15\approx 0.93\).
Clear the decimals. Multiply the top and the bottom by the same power of 10: \(0.008/0.107=8/107\), a little less than \(8/100\), so about \(0.075\).
Products of decimals. Multiply the digits, then count the decimal places: \(0.03\times 0.7=0.021\) and \(0.25\times 0.36=0.09\).
Dividing by a simple decimal. Dividing by 0.5 is multiplying by 2; by 0.25, by 4; by 0.2, by 5; by 0.4, by 2.5.
Powers. Square, then square again: \(0.9^2=0.81\) and \(0.9^4=0.81^2=0.6561\); \(0.7^2=0.49\) and \(0.7^3=0.343\). A power of \(\tfrac12\) is \(1/2^n\).
Square roots. Look for a perfect square first: \(\sqrt{2.25}=1.5\), \(\sqrt{0.0016}=0.04\). Otherwise bracket the root between two squares you know: \(1.1^2=1.21\) and \(1.2^2=1.44\), so \(\sqrt{1.3}\) is about 1.14.
Multiplying by 1.96. \(1.96\,\sigma=2\sigma-0.04\,\sigma\). For example, \(1.96\times 15=30-0.6=29.4\).
Logs and the sigmoid. The logistic problem gives a table of \(\sigma(z)\) and \(\log\sigma(z)\). For \(1-p\), flip the sign of \(z\): if \(p=\sigma(2)=0.88\), then \(1-p=\sigma(-2)=0.12\), and \(-\log(1-p)=-\log\sigma(-2)=2.1\).
Values the exam gives you. If a part needs a power that is slow by hand, such as \(0.97^{20}\), the problem states its value. Use it.

title: AII 600 midterm study guide
section: What to put on your cheat sheet
text:
What to put on your cheat sheet
Write the sheet yourself: making it is studying. A suggested list, one block per section:

Probability. Complement; addition rule; \(P(A\mid B)=P(A\text{ and }B)/P(B)\); multiplication rule; the independence test; total probability; Bayes rule; posterior odds \(=\) Bayes factor \(\times\) prior odds; \(P=O/(1+O)\) for odds in favor.
Expectation and variance. \(E(X)=\sum x\,p(x)\); \(Var(X)=E(X^2)-E(X)^2\); \(Cov\) and \(Corr\); \(E(aX+bY)\) and \(Var(aX+bY)\) with the covariance term; a sum of \(n\) independent draws has mean \(n\mu\) and standard deviation \(\sqrt n\,\sigma\), and an average has \(\mu\) and \(\sigma/\sqrt n\); total expectation.
Binomial. The four conditions; \(P(X=x)=\binom nx p^x(1-p)^{n-x}\); \(np\); \(np(1-p)\); \(sd(\hat p)=\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}\).
Normal. \(z=(x-\mu)/\sigma\); 95% lies within \(\mu\pm 1.96\sigma\), so 2.5% in each tail and 50% on each side of \(\mu\); rank tail probabilities by comparing \(z\)-values; the level exceeded only 2.5% of the time is \(\mu+1.96\sigma\); the central limit theorem.
Regression. \(\hat b\) and \(\hat a\); \(e=y-\hat y\); \(SSE\) and \(J=SSE/(2n)\); the influence \(\Delta(x_i-\bar x)/S_{xx}\); \(\hat y\pm 1.96\hat\sigma\); \(e/\hat\sigma\); least squares equals maximum likelihood under normal errors; the residual-plot table.
Logistic regression. \(z=\beta_0+\beta_1x\); \(p=\sigma(z)=1/(1+e^{-z})\); \(\sigma(-z)=1-\sigma(z)\); \(z=\log\frac{p}{1-p}\); a coefficient changes the log-odds, and \(e^{\beta}\) multiplies the odds; log loss \(-y\log p-(1-y)\log(1-p)\); \(P(Y=y\mid p)=p^y(1-p)^{1-y}\), so the total log loss is minus the log-likelihood.
Arithmetic. The squares from \(1^2\) to \(20^2\), so you recognize a perfect square such as \(2.25=1.5^2\), and \(1.96\,\sigma=2\sigma-0.04\,\sigma\).
One worked example per section, in your own handwriting.

title: AII 600 midterm study guide
text:
Mistakes that cost points

Dividing by the wrong total in a conditional probability.
Confusing \(P(A\mid B)\) with \(P(B\mid A)\), including the prosecutor’s fallacy.
Leaving the base rate out of Bayes rule.
Multiplying probabilities without independence, or adding probabilities of events that overlap.
Dropping the covariance term, or forgetting to square the weights, in a variance.
Using the variance where the standard deviation belongs, in a \(z\)-score or in \(N(\mu,\sigma^2)\).
Putting all 5% in one tail: 95% within \(\pm 1.96\sigma\) leaves 2.5% on each side.
Writing the standard deviation of a sum of \(n\) draws as \(n\sigma\) instead of \(\sqrt n\,\sigma\).
Reading a slope as a causal effect, or an intercept as meaningful outside the data.
Calling a case an outlier without its standardized residual.
Reading a logistic coefficient as a change in probability, or using \(p\) instead of \(1-p\) in the log loss when \(y=0\).
A number with no sentence. Every exam problem asks what the number means.
